pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the rescue in this workspace. Share it with the rescue coordinator, the foster manager, the adoption counselors and the medical volunteers.
: animals you have agreed to take from shelters, the pull-by date, and whether a foster is ready.
: every animal from intake to adoption, with where it came from, sex, weight, altered and vaccine status, microchip, who it is good with, the fee and notes.
: every foster, what they take, how many at once, who lives there, and how many animals are with them now.
: exams, vaccines, surgery and treatment, with cost and who is driving.
: every family, with the reference, landlord, home visit, contract and fee.
Monday: pulls for the week confirmed against foster room.
Through the week: intake exams within a day of arrival; vet visits driven.
Wednesday: the adoption team reviews new applications and checks.
Every morning: pulls due, vet visits today, new applications
Every Monday: animals not yet altered, fosters with room
Every month: vet spending, adoptions, average weeks in care
Every quarter: foster thank-yous and recruiting

The rescue coordinator says yes to pulls. The foster manager places animals and supports fosters. Adoption counselors run applications. Medical volunteers book and drive vet visits, and the board treasurer reads vet spending each month.
Applicants' and fosters' phone numbers and emails are private. Share this workspace with your team, not with every volunteer. Microchip numbers move to the adopter's name on adoption day.
Rename species, sources and shelters to match your rescue and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place and drag cards between columns; every count updates on its own.
The rescue at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

text.text: The first 72 hours decide how fast an animal is adopted. A complete intake means no surprises later: no missing vaccine, no unknown health problem, no foster who was told the wrong thing.

Vaccines: dogs get distemper-parvo and rabies when old enough; cats get the combination vaccine and rabies.
Tests: heartworm for dogs over six months; FIV and FeLV for cats.

Waffles arrives from the county shelter with no records. The coordinator logs him as a shelter pull, the medical volunteer drives him to the intake exam the same day, and he goes to the Calloway house. Two weeks later he is neutered, chipped and vaccinated, and his foster's notes say he loves children.
A good adoption matches the animal's real needs to the family's real life. Be warm, be quick, and never skip the checks: returns are hard on everyone, most of all the animal.
The adoption counselor replies within one day, even if only to say it is being read.
called: the family's vet if they have had pets, or a personal reference
in writing for renters, or "Not needed" for owners
done, in person or by video: fences, other pets, where the animal will sleep
A conversation with the foster, who knows the animal best

Talk about the family's day: who is home, how active they are, children's ages, other pets. Read the foster's notes together. If the match is poor, say so kindly and suggest a better fit; many families adopt a different animal they had not considered.
. Other applicants for the same animal get a personal note and an invitation to meet others.
signed: return to the rescue if it does not work out, never to a shelter
Microchip registration moved to the new family
Medical records, food for a few days and the foster's notes handed over
Call at three days, three weeks and three months. Most problems show up early and are easy to solve with advice. A family who asks to return an animal is helped, never shamed.

Moose, a big shepherd mix, has two applications. One family lives in an apartment with no yard; the other has a fenced yard and older children. After checks and a home visit, the second family is approved, the first is invited to meet a smaller dog, and Moose goes home the following Saturday.
Fosters are the rescue. Without a building, every animal you save lives in someone's home. Look after fosters and they will foster for years.

to see who has room. A home with young children is not the place for a dog that has not been tested with children. Medical cases go only to experienced fosters.
Fosters burn out. Offer a break after every two or three animals, and move a home to
without any guilt. A rested foster comes back.

and celebrate milestones: the fifth, the tenth, the fiftieth animal.

The Nwosu-Bennett family fosters a litter of four kittens. The rescue drops off food, litter and a pen, the medical volunteer collects the kittens for their vaccines, and the family writes notes every Sunday. Eight weeks later all four are adopted, and the family asks for a break before the next litter.
